events.text: The first thing you know is cold. The second is water: a spring that wells up through white sand among the roots of a birch, so clear that the stones on the bottom look close enough to lick, and you try. Ice round the edge stones. A great grey-white shape curled round you like a wall, breathing slowly, and on its brow a single horn, pale as a white candle, giving off in the half-dark a little light of its own.
events.arc: The Spring at the Edge of the World

choices.text: Drink

effects.log: The water is so cold it rings in your teeth. It tastes of nothing at all, which, you will learn, is the rarest taste in the world. (+2 Clarity)

choices.text: Look up at the horn

effects.log: You stare until your eyes water. Your mother lowers her head so the horn is close, and lets you look. On your own brow, under the curls, there is a bump the size of a pine nut, and it itches. You do not know yet that it is the same thing.

choices.text: Shake your head, hard

effects.log: You shake your head and fall over. Something on your brow makes a sound, very faint, like a bead of ice dropped on a stone. Your mother's ears go up. She has heard that sound before, a long time ago, from her own brow.

events.text: Night at the spring. Wolves on the ridge, an owl, the creak of birches in the frost. Your mother does not sleep the way other beasts sleep. She sits so still that the snow settles on her mane and does not melt, and by morning she is a grey stone with a horn. Then the stone yawns.
events.arc: The Spring at the Edge of the World

choices.text: Sit beside her, as still as you can

effects.log: You last as long as it takes one snowflake to melt on your nose. Then you sneeze. But for that long the forest was very loud and very clear, and every sound in it was exactly what it was. (+2 Clarity)

choices.text: Burrow into her mane and sleep like a kid

effects.log: Her mane is warm all the way down, and smells of snow and bitter leaves. You sleep. In the morning there is a little drift of snow on top of you both, and she has not moved once all night, so as not to wake you.

choices.text: Watch the wolves come down to drink

effects.log: The wolves come to the far side of the spring at moonset. They look at the stone with the horn, drink quickly, and go. Nothing on this mountain drinks slowly near a haechi. You file that away.

events.text: On the stream below the spring, a fox in a red winter coat is talking to a hare. The fox is very kind. The river is frozen right across, it says; the far bank is all clover under the snow; it would go itself, only its paw is bad. The hare looks at the ice. The bud on your brow goes cold, so cold it aches, and in your mouth, from nowhere, there is a taste like salt.
events.arc: The Spring at the Edge of the World

choices.text: Bleat as loud as a kid can

effects.log: The hare jumps a body-length straight up and runs, up the bank and away from the ice. The fox looks at you for a long moment with its head on one side. It has never been interrupted by a goat before. You are not a goat. It will find that out.

choices.text: Look at your mother

effects.log: She is already up. She walks down to the stream without hurrying and stands on the bank with her head low, and the fox remembers somewhere else to be. "That," she says, in the low rumble that is a haechi's voice, "is what a lie tastes like. Remember the salt."

choices.text: Hold the salt on your tongue and wonder at it

effects.log: The hare goes out onto the ice, and the ice holds, and holds, and at the dark water in the middle the hare stops, sniffs, and turns back. It caught the lie by itself. Hares are not stupid. The salt fades off your tongue slowly, like a word. (+2 Clarity)

events.text: The ice goes out of the stream with a noise like a hundred doors. You stand at the spring and practise the salt. The stream says it is running: true. The wind says it is spring: true, nearly. A jay says the acorns under the big larch are its own: true, and rather smug about it. The fox, passing, wishes you a good morning, and the bud goes cold. It is not a good morning for somebody, somewhere, and the fox knows it.
events.arc: The Spring at the Edge of the World

choices.text: Follow the fox

ok.log: It goes to the foot of the tall birch where the magpie nests, sits, and looks up at the nest for a long, thoughtful time. Then it sees you and starts talking about the weather. You will remember this tree.

fail.log: You lose it in the first ferns and then lose yourself in the second. By the time you find the stream again it is dark, and your own spring has never looked so beautiful. (-4 health)

choices.text: Stay at the spring and keep practising

effects.log: All day: true, true, true, salt, true. By evening you can taste the difference before the speaker has finished the sentence, and the bud on your brow is a little longer. (+2 Clarity)

choices.text: Tell the jay its acorns are being watched

effects.log: You stand under the larch and stamp until the jay comes down to scold you, and then you look at the squirrel in the next tree, hard. The jay is not stupid either. That evening it moves its acorns.

events.text: Your mother teaches you the first thing; the only thing, she says, that matters. She lowers her head, slowly, until the white horn points at an old birch stump. "Never at the innocent," she says. "Not once. A horn that has been lowered at the innocent is never quite clean again." Then she makes you do it, at the stump, a hundred times.

choices.text: Practise until your neck aches

effects.log: A hundred times, and then a hundred more, because the first hundred were sloppy. By evening your neck aches and the stump has a small white scuff on it at exactly the height of a kid's brow.

choices.text: Ask how you will know who is guilty

effects.log: "You will taste it." "And if I do not?" She looks at you for a long time. "Then you lie down," she says, "and you do not lower your head at anyone. Better no butt than a wrong one." You will need this more than you know.

choices.text: Butt the stump properly

effects.log: You run at it. The stump wins. You sit in the moss seeing stars, and your mother says, without any expression at all, that the stump was innocent too. (-3 health)

events.text: An old man comes up the stream with a knife and a bundle of birch bark, lost, a long way from any village. He sees your mother, and the horn, and stands quite still. "I am only an old bark-peeler," he says, "and I have lost my way, and my knees are bad, and I mean nobody any harm." Every word of it tastes of plain cold water. Your mother lays her ears flat back against her skull, and bows her great head to him.

choices.text: Lay your ears back and bow with her

effects.log: Your ears do not go flat yet; they flop. You bow anyway. The old man looks from one of you to the other and, very slowly, bows back. Then your mother walks him down to the path, and he follows her as if she were a lantern.

choices.text: Go and sniff him

effects.log: Birch sap, millet, pipe ash, tired feet. Nothing sour. He laughs and lets you chew his sleeve, and leaves a twist of salt on the edge stone that your mother will not let you lick.

choices.text: Stare at his face, to learn what upright looks like

effects.log: It looks like nothing much: a lined face, a wet nose, a bit of bark in the beard. "Upright does not look like anything," your mother says afterward. "That is why the horn is needed."

events.text: On the slope above the spring stands a crooked tree with grey bark and long feathery leaves, and clusters of pale berries that hang on all winter like little beads. It should not grow this far north; your mother says a haechi carried its seed up from the south in its mane, a very long time ago. She eats its leaves. Nothing else on the mountain eats them. When she makes you try one, it tastes like a punishment.

choices.text: Chew, swallow, and keep chewing

effects.log: Your mouth goes numb, then your throat, then your whole head, very clean and very cold, as if someone had opened a window in it. Your mother watches you not spit, and says nothing, which is praise. (+3 Clarity, -2 health)

choices.text: Spit it out and eat the sweet moss instead

effects.log: The moss is soft and sweet and full of little white flowers. That night the bud on your brow itches dully, like a word you cannot remember. (-1 Clarity)

choices.text: Ask why

effects.log: "Sweet things want something from you," she says. "Bitter things do not." Then she eats another leaf, as calmly as if it were honey, and you have the feeling that is not the whole answer.

events.text: Two trappers come up the stream in the first snow: brothers, by their faces, the elder in a fox-fur hat, the younger thin from a winter's cough in the hut. At the spring, while the younger drinks, the elder tells him the traps took only five sables all season, and the price will be poor. There are seven pelts inside his coat. The bud on your brow goes cold, and your mother stands up out of the snow.

choices.text: Watch what she does

effects.log: She walks between them, lowers her head at the elder, and nudges him, not hard. His coat falls open and seven sables slide into the snow. The younger looks at them for a long time. Your mother lies down again. "I did not punish him," she tells you later. "I only showed. What the brother does with it is the brother's."

choices.text: Go first, before she can

ok.log: You put your small head down and run at the elder's knees. He sits down hard in the snow, and seven sables spill out of his coat. The younger brother stares at them, and then at you. Your mother does not move. When they are gone she licks your brow once, over the bud. Your first true butt.

fail.log: You slip on the ice of the edge stone and land on your chin. Your mother steps over you and does it properly: a nudge, a coat falling open, seven sables in the snow. You will be faster next time. (-3 health)

choices.text: Hide behind the birch. It is not your quarrel

effects.log: From behind the birch you see your mother show the younger brother the pelts, and you see something else: the younger brother is not surprised. He knew. He only wanted someone else to say it.

events.text: One winter morning your mother walks north up the frozen stream, as she sometimes does, to sit the Stone Sleep on the ridge where the larches end. She does not come back in spring. She does not come back in summer. In autumn you climb to the ridge. There is a grey stone there in the shape of a lying beast, snow on its back, and on its brow a smooth place where a horn could have been, or not. The spring below is yours now. Nobody has to tell you.

choices.text: Lie down beside the stone for a winter

effects.log: A whole winter on the ridge with your flank against the cold stone. It does not move, and you do not ask it to. In spring you walk down to the spring alone, and keep it, and it is yours. (+4 Clarity, -6 health)

choices.text: Go back down and keep the spring clean, as she did

effects.log: Dead leaves out, a drowned beetle out, the silt raked off the white sand with your hoof. By the first snow the water is so clear that the bottom looks close enough to touch. It is yours. (+2 Clarity)

choices.text: Shake your head at the stone until your bud rings

effects.log: It rings, thin as ice. And from somewhere very far to the north, very faint, something rings back. Or the river ice cracked. You decide, and go on deciding all your life, that it was not the ice.

events.text: A fox from the stream has decided you are interesting. It sits on a log across the spring and talks. It talks to everything: to the magpie about the squirrel, to the squirrel about the magpie, to the hare about the weather, and to the weather, you suspect, about the hare. Every third thing it says tastes of salt. "Little horn," it says to you, warmly, "what a fine beast you will be. Everyone in the forest says so." Nobody in the forest says so.

choices.text: Lower your head at it, just to see

effects.log: It is a lie, but a small one, and the fox only laughs and moves its log two lengths further off. You have learned that the fox knows exactly what a horn is. That is worth knowing.

choices.text: Say nothing and listen to everything it says, all afternoon

effects.log: Twenty things. Seven of them salt. And the seven are not scattered: they gather, like flies, round the magpie and the tall birch where the magpie nests.

choices.text: Ask it why it lies

effects.log: "Lie?" The fox is wounded to the heart. "I tell stories. A fox without stories is only a dog." That, your bud informs you, is true. The fox seems pleased that you noticed.

events.text: A young roe deer at the stream, nervous, alone for the first time. The fox, from its log: "The wolves went east this morning, little one. Go west, by the dead larches. Lovely grazing." The wolves went west. You smelled them at dawn. The fox has an interest in what the wolves leave behind.

choices.text: Step into the deer's path: the fox says the wolves went east (the horn: a lie)

effects.log: You stand across the path to the dead larches with your bud pointed at the fox, and the deer, who has never seen a haechi, decides that east looks lovely after all. The fox sighs. "One day," it says, "you will be a terrible nuisance to everyone."

choices.text: Bleat a warning at the deer

ok.log: The deer looks at you, at the fox, at you, and goes east. Deer are not clever, but they know which of two faces is smiling too much.

fail.log: The deer bolts the wrong way. You run after it, and get between it and the wolves' smell just in time, and both of you run home very fast. (-3 health)

choices.text: Ask the fox where the wolves really are

effects.log: "East," says the fox again, very sincerely, and then, when you keep looking at it: "North-east." Salt, and salt. A liar, you learn, lies the second time in the same direction as the first. The deer, bored, wanders off south and is perfectly safe.

events.text: The magpie in the tall birch has lost her eggs, all five, and is telling the whole forest. She lands on the edge stone of your spring and demands that you, the beast with the horn, do something. The squirrel was near the nest, she says. The fox, sitting very neatly on its log, agrees: it saw the squirrel at dawn with yolk on its whiskers. The squirrel chatters from a high branch that it was at the far pines all morning. Everyone looks at you.

choices.text: The fox saw yolk on the squirrel's whiskers (the horn: a lie). Lower your head at the fox

effects.log: The salt is so strong it makes your eyes run. You put your head down and walk at the fox, and the fox, who has never in its life been walked at, goes backwards off the log into the stream. There is yolk on its whiskers. The magpie says a great many things. Your first true butt.

choices.text: The horn is only a dull itch. Lower your head at the fox anyway, on a hunch

ok.log: A hunch, and the way the fox said "yolk" a little too quickly. You walk at it, and it goes backwards into the stream, and there is yolk on its whiskers. The horn did not tell you. You told the horn. Your first true butt.

fail.log: The fox simply steps aside, and you walk straight into the stream. By the time you climb out, everyone has gone home, and the eggs are still gone. At least you did not lower your head at the squirrel.

choices.text: Lower your head at the squirrel. It was near the nest

effects.log: You butt the squirrel's tree until it falls out, and it limps away under everyone's eyes, a thief. That evening you see the fox licking yolk off its whiskers. Something in your horn cracks, very quietly. (A crack: -8 Clarity)

choices.text: Lie down. The horn has not said, so you will not

effects.log: The magpie calls you useless, and the fox smiles very kindly, and the eggs stay gone. Better no butt than a wrong one. It does not feel better. It only is.

events.text: The fox comes to the spring in a lean winter, thin, a few grey hairs in its muzzle, and sits a long way off. "I have been thinking about your horn," it says. "It cannot tell what is true. It can only tell what I believe is false. If I believe a thing, little horn, you cannot catch me in it, even when the thing is wrong." Your bud stays quiet. For once the fox is telling the truth, and it knows that you know.

choices.text: Think about that for a long time

effects.log: A fool cannot lie to you, and a fool can still be wrong. Error is not a lie. The most dangerous witness, you think, lying awake, would be an honest one who is mistaken, and a horn would bow to them.

choices.text: Share your spring with it this winter

effects.log: It drinks every evening at the far side. In return it tells you three true things about the forest, and one lie, out of habit, and then apologises for the lie, which is a thing you did not know a fox could do.

choices.text: Chase it off. A fox is a fox

effects.log: It goes, without hurry, over the snow. At the edge of the trees it stops and looks back. "That," it calls, "was honest of you." It is the last thing it ever says to you that does not taste of salt.

events.text: The magpie has laid again, higher this time, and lost them again. This time she does not scream. She comes down to your spring and sits on the edge stone, smooths her feathers, and says, very formally, that she has a case. She says it as if it were the most ordinary thing in the world.

choices.text: Hear the case, properly, lying down

effects.log: You lie down with your head up and your ears forward, the way you once saw it done. The magpie seems to find this correct. She begins at the beginning, which in a magpie's case is three summers ago.

choices.text: Tell her you are only a kid

effects.log: "And I am only a magpie," she says. "We shall manage." She begins at the beginning, which is three summers ago.

choices.text: Ask who she accuses

effects.log: "The squirrel," she says at once. "It is always the squirrel." She says it without salt. She believes it. That, you remind yourself, is not the same as its being so.

events.text: The hearing, at the foot of the tall birch. The squirrel swears it was at the far pines all morning. The snake on the bough below the nest says nothing at all; snakes rarely do. The magpie glares at the squirrel. The whole forest, in the ferns, waits to see where the little horn will point.

choices.text: The squirrel says it was at the far pines (the horn: a lie). Ask it where it really was

effects.log: It was in the jay's acorn store, it admits, with its tail very small. Not near the nest at all. The horn found the lie, and the lie was about acorns. The horn reads lies, not guilt. You will remember the difference.

choices.text: Lower your head at the squirrel: it is lying about something

effects.log: You butt its tree, and it tumbles out, and confesses at once: the jay's acorns. Not the eggs. It is a true butt, at the wrong crime, and the magpie goes on glaring at it. Your horn does not crack. It only feels foolish. (-2 Clarity)

choices.text: Turn to the snake and wait for it to speak

effects.log: It does not speak. It does not lie, either. It simply looks at you, a long time, with eyes that never close, and you understand that a horn has nothing to read in a creature that says nothing.

events.text: Another clutch, and this time you watch the tall birch all night instead of asking anyone anything. In the hour before dawn something long goes up the bark like water running the wrong way. In the morning the nest is empty and the snake is lying on its bough, very round in the middle, saying nothing.

choices.text: Lower your head at the snake: it never said a word, but you saw

effects.log: You butt the trunk until the snake slides off its bough and goes away over the ferns, round and slow and unrepentant. The magpie builds her next nest in a thorn tree. No horn read anything; your eyes did. It counts.

choices.text: Tell the magpie, and let the birds settle it

effects.log: The magpie calls her cousins, all of them, and for a week the snake cannot cross the forest without forty magpies telling it what they think of it. That is a kind of court too.

choices.text: Leave it. A snake that eats eggs is not a liar, only a snake

effects.log: It told no lie. It did what snakes do. A haechi is for the ones who are in the wrong, and you are not sure, lying by the spring that night, that a hungry snake is in the wrong. The magpie is sure. The magpie is not a haechi.

events.text: Autumn, and the wild mountain grapes are ripe on the vines that climb the oaks by the stream: small, dark, so sweet the wasps go silly on them, and every bear and boy in the forest knows it. They hang low enough for a young haechi to reach. The bitter tree on the slope above is exactly as bitter as it was yesterday.

choices.text: Eat grapes, all autumn

effects.log: Your muzzle goes purple and stays purple. You sleep well and wake hungry for more. Somewhere toward the first frost you notice the bud on your brow feels thick, like a tongue after honey. (-5 Clarity)

choices.text: Eat some grapes, and the bitter leaf after them

effects.log: Sweet in the afternoon, bitter at dusk to wash it out. It almost works. The bud on your brow feels a little thick in the mornings. (-1 Clarity)

choices.text: Leave them to the bears. Chew the bitter leaf

effects.log: The bears are delighted. Your mouth is numb all autumn, and the forest, when it talks, is very clear. (+2 Clarity)

events.text: Winter, and something is wrong. The fox tells the hare a lie and you cannot taste it. A woodpecker tells you the ice on the stream is thin, which it is, and you think it is lying, and walk out onto it, and go through. Your bud is thick and warm and tells you nothing. You stand in the shallows, soaked to the shoulder, and think about grapes.

choices.text: Go back to the bitter tree and chew until your mouth is numb

effects.log: A week of leaves so bitter you weep. On the eighth morning the fox says good morning, and it tastes of salt, and you could kiss the fox. You do not. (+6 Clarity, -4 health)

choices.text: Wash the horn in the spring, over and over

effects.log: You put your head under the cold water until your ears ache, and hold it there, and the warmth goes out of the bud a little at a time. (+4 Clarity)

choices.text: Eat the last frozen grapes. The horn will come back on its own

effects.log: They are wonderful frozen. The horn does not come back on its own. It stays thick until spring, and you believe two lies and doubt one truth, and you are not sure which were which. (-3 Clarity)

events.text: You lie under the bitter tree in the first snow and understand, at last, what the old haechi meant. Sweet things want something from you. The grape wants you to carry its seed. The fox's kindness wants your silence. A bitter leaf wants nothing, and so it cannot buy you, and so the horn stays clean.

choices.text: Carry a handful of its berries to plant beside your spring

effects.log: You bury them in the soft earth by the outflow, the way a haechi once carried them north in its mane. One comes up in spring, crooked and stubborn, exactly like its parent. (+2 Clarity)

choices.text: Eat the leaf every day from now on, whether you want to or not

effects.log: It never gets nicer. It only gets more yours. (+3 Clarity)

choices.text: Sit under it a whole season and think

effects.log: What else is sweet? Praise. Being needed. Being right. You do not have answers yet. You have a tree, and it is very bitter, and you are fond of it.

events.text: A hut of larch logs on the stream below, chimney smoke, four trappers wintering for sable. The pelts go south to the county as tribute, because the court is always short of sable, and whatever is over goes across the river at night to men who pay in silver and do not ask. Tonight they found your tracks. "A haechi horn," says the eldest, turning a pelt over and over, "is worth a hundred sables to an alchemist in the south. They grind it." {npc}, the youngest, who sets the traps nobody else will walk to, says nothing, and puts another log on the fire.

choices.text: Leave the valley for the winter

effects.log: You go over the ridge to a colder spring and a worse winter, and come back in the thaw to find the hut empty and your spring untouched. Somebody stepped round it carefully, every time.

choices.text: Walk past the hut by moonlight, close, and let them see the horn

effects.log: Four faces at the one window. Nobody comes out. In the morning, three of them argue about whether it was real. {npc} does not argue. {He} looks at your tracks for a long time.

choices.text: Watch {npc}

effects.log: {npc} walks the far trapline alone, talks to the snow, and once stops at a snare with a living sable in it, looks round, and lets it go. Nobody else will ever know. You know.

events.text: Spring, and the split of the pelts in front of the hut. Thirty pelts on the bench, says the eldest, and four spoiled by the damp, so twenty-six shares, the eldest's the largest, as is right. {npc} counts the bench twice with {his} eyes and says nothing. You are lying in the birches, close enough to taste every word.

choices.text: The eldest says four were spoiled by the damp (the horn: a lie). Walk into the light and lower your head at the eldest

effects.log: Four men freeze. You walk past three of them and lower your head at the eldest, and the eldest steps back into the hut door, and the pack on the peg falls, and four perfect sables slide out of it. Nobody says anything for a long time. Then {npc} counts again, out loud, to thirty.

choices.text: Your horn is dull with winter. Lower your head at the one who talks loudest, on a guess

ok.log: The loudest is the eldest, and the loudest is the liar; it is not always so. The eldest's pack falls, four sables slide out, and you walk back into the birches with your heart going like a hare's.

fail.log: The loudest is the second brother, shouting because that one counted thirty too. You lower your head at an honest man, and the eldest laughs and points: even the beast says so. Something in your horn cracks, very quietly. (A crack: -8 Clarity)

choices.text: Show {npc} where the four pelts are: nose the eldest's pack in the night

effects.log: {npc} wakes to find a horned beast nosing a pack on the peg, and does not shout. In the morning {he} says nothing to anyone. But {his} share that spring is a fair one, and the eldest cannot work out why.

choices.text: Stay in the birches. It is their quarrel

effects.log: The shares are split, unfairly. {npc} takes {his} without a word and walks away up the stream, and stops, a little way off, and looks straight at the birch you are lying behind.

events.text: A smell of cold iron on the path to your spring. A wire snare, cleverly set at the height of a young haechi's neck, between two birches you always pass between. The eldest trapper's work: you know those hands by now, and that sweat. At dawn, a figure comes up the path with a knife. It is {npc}.

choices.text: Step out and watch what {npc} does

mem.note: cut the eldest's snare off the haechi's path

effects.log: {npc} sees you, goes white, and then, with shaking hands, cuts the wire and coils it and puts it in {his} coat. "I never saw you," {he} says, to the air. It is a lie, a kind one, and your bud does not even tingle.

choices.text: Break the snare yourself before {npc} reaches it

ok.log: You set your horn bud under the wire and heave, and the birch it is tied to cracks. {npc} arrives to find a broken tree and a broken snare, and laughs out loud in the empty forest.

fail.log: The wire bites into your foreleg before it gives. {npc} finds you tangled and frees you with the knife, swearing softly the whole time, and binds the leg with a strip of {his} own sleeve. (-10 health)

choices.text: Go round by the ridge and leave them all to it

effects.log: You never use that path again. The snare hangs there empty until it rusts, and the eldest trapper tells the inn at the county town that the haechi is too clever for wire. That makes it worth more.

events.text: Years on. A new crew winters in the larch hut, and the eldest of them now is {npc}, broad and slow and grey at the temples. You hear {him} at the fire: "Not this valley. Trap the next one. And if you see tracks with one scrape between the hoofprints, you go round." A young trapper asks why. {npc} takes a long time to answer.

choices.text: Walk into the firelight and lay your ears back to {him}

mem.note: bowed to me at the fire

effects.log: The young ones scramble back. {npc} does not move. You lay your ears flat and bow your head to an honest trapper, and {npc} bows back, slowly, the way you once saw an old bark-peeler do. No one at that fire ever sets a snare in your valley.

choices.text: Stay in the dark and listen to the answer

effects.log: "Because it knows," {npc} says at last, "and I would rather be known than rich." The young ones laugh. {npc} does not. You lie in the dark a long time after the fire goes down.

choices.text: Leave the valley to them for good. It is time

effects.log: You go before dawn. Behind you, {npc} will tell the story of the beast with one horn until {he} is very old, and get it almost right.

events.text: A dry summer: no rain since the snow went, the moss crisp underfoot, the stream down to a thread. In the afternoon the sky goes the colour of a bruise. Lightning strikes the tallest larch on the ridge, and the larch stands there burning like a torch for a long breath, and then the fire goes down into the dry grass and begins to run.

choices.text: Run to the spring

effects.log: You run as fast as a young haechi can run, and stand in the spring up to your belly, and watch the ridge turn orange. Every creature on the mountain has had the same idea. A hare stands between your forelegs, trembling, and you let it.

choices.text: Stay beside your mother and do what she does

effects.log: She does not run. She walks to the edge of the slope above the spring and lies down facing the fire, ears flat, and watches it come, the way you have seen her watch a liar.

choices.text: Run toward the fire to see it

effects.log: It is louder than anything. It eats the air. A gust throws sparks in your face and your mane smoulders, and you are back at the spring before you remember deciding to run. (-6 health)

events.text: The fire comes down to the edge of the slope above the spring, where the bitter tree stands. Your mother gets up. She walks into the burning grass, takes a burning larch branch in her jaws as if it were a stick, and swallows the fire off it: you see it go down her throat, a long red light, and then the branch is only black wood. She does it again. And again. Her eyes are streaming. The fire stops at the bitter tree.

choices.text: Bring her water in your mouth from the spring

effects.log: Mouthful after mouthful, up the slope, spilling half. She drinks from your mouth like a kid, which is the wrong way round, and goes back to the fire. By dawn your legs will not hold you. (-3 health)

choices.text: Watch, and remember every move

effects.log: Head low, jaws wide, the breath held, the fire taken in on the out-breath. You see it, and you will never forget it. You do not understand yet that it hurts her.

choices.text: Hide in the spring with the hare

effects.log: You put your head under the water every time the fire roars. When you come up, the fire is out, and your mother is lying by the bitter tree, coughing smoke, very tired.

events.text: One branch is still burning near the stream, a small one, the right size for a young haechi. Your mother is coughing by the bitter tree and does not see it. It is creeping toward the dry moss along the bank, where the ground birds nest.

choices.text: Do what she did. Take it in your jaws and swallow the fire

ok.log: It goes down like a hot coal and sits in your belly glowing. Smoke comes out of your nose for three days. The moss does not burn. Your mother looks at you for a long time and says only, "Not yet. Not for a hundred years." (-8 health, -3 Clarity)

fail.log: You get a mouthful of smoke and spit the branch out burning into the stream, which puts it out, which is a kind of success. Your tongue blisters, your eyes stream, and your bud is full of smoke for a month. (-12 health, -3 Clarity)

choices.text: Kick it into the stream

effects.log: A hiss, a curl of steam, a black stick floating away. Less heroic than swallowing it, and it works just as well. Your mother, coughing, makes a sound that might be a laugh.

choices.text: Stay back. You are afraid of it

effects.log: You stand in the spring and watch the branch crawl toward the moss, and your legs will not move. Your mother sees it at the last moment and puts it out with one hoof. You will be afraid of fire for a long time. Some fear is only good sense.

events.text: Spring after the fire. The ridge is black, with green already coming through the ash, and the spring is grey: ash on the water, ash in the sand, a dead jay in the outflow. It tastes of smoke. The haechi who bore you is coughing still, and leaves the spring to you.

choices.text: Clear it, stone by stone, until the bottom shows

effects.log: Ash out, the jay out, the sand raked clean with your hoof and then raked again. It takes a whole season. In the autumn the water is so clear the stones look close enough to touch. You did it alone. It is yours. (+3 Clarity)

choices.text: Find a new spring under the unburned side of the hill

ok.log: Under a tumble of mossy rocks on the north side, a thread of water so cold it hurts. You dig it out, and widen it, and it becomes a pool, and the pool becomes yours. (+3 Clarity)

fail.log: You find a spring, and it is sour with iron and a dead deer upstream. You drink once, and spit, and go back to the grey one. (-4 health)

choices.text: Drink the smoky water. It will clear on its own

effects.log: It clears by the next spring, more or less. You do not, quite. All year the world tastes faintly of burning, and every lie has smoke in it. (-2 Clarity)

events.text: At the forest's edge, where the hill pastures begin, a hamlet of five houses keeps goats and a few fat-tailed sheep bought across the river. A herder, {npc}, comes up into your trees with a crook and a sour face, calling a lost ewe. "The neighbour's dog took that ewe," {he} tells the forest, loudly, as if the forest might be asked later. "Everyone will see. That yellow dog took it."

choices.text: Follow {npc} down, keeping to the trees

effects.log: You keep to the trees. {npc} stops once at {his} own pen and looks inside, quickly, and then goes on to the headman's gate. You would like very much to see inside that pen.

choices.text: Taste the words again, from closer

effects.log: You come out of the birches and stand in the path, and {npc} stops dead and stares at the bud on your brow. "The dog," {he} says again, weaker. It tastes of salt, even to a kid's horn. {He} goes down the hill much faster than {he} came up.

choices.text: It is a herder's quarrel. Go back to the spring

effects.log: You go back to your spring. That evening you hear a dog howling in the hamlet below, the howl of a dog that has been chained up and does not know why.

events.text: The hamlet's headman hears the case under the elm by the well: {npc}'s lost ewe, the neighbour's yellow dog, a price in grain if the dog is guilty, and the dog sent away to the county. The neighbour is a widow with a bad hip who has nothing but the dog. Then somebody sees you standing at the edge of the elm's shade, and everyone stops talking at once.

choices.text: {npc} swears the dog took the ewe (the horn: a lie). Lower your head at {npc}

effects.log: You walk through them all and lower your head at {npc}, gently, and {he} steps back against the wattle of {his} own pen, and the gate swings open, and out walks the ewe, fat and offended, chewing. Nobody says a word. Then the widow begins to laugh.

choices.text: The horn is dull. Go and sniff the pens

ok.log: You walk past every pen in the hamlet with your nose down, and stop at {npc}'s, and stand there until somebody looks in. The ewe is in the back, behind the hay. It was a truth told with the nose. It counts.

fail.log: Goat, goat, hay, goat, and too many smells for a young nose. You find nothing. The headman sends the yellow dog away to the county, and the widow sits by the well all evening. You did not do it. You did not stop it.

choices.text: Lower your head at the dog: there is wool in its teeth

effects.log: Wool in its teeth from the widow's own old coat. You lower your head at it, and the hamlet takes that for a verdict, and the dog is sent away, and the widow limps home alone. That night your horn aches. A crack. (-8 Clarity)

choices.text: Lie down beside the dog so nobody can take it

effects.log: Nobody wants to take a dog from beside a beast with a horn. The headman puts the matter off till autumn. By autumn, quietly, {npc}'s pen has one more ewe in it than anyone counted, and nobody mentions the dog again.

events.text: {npc} comes up to your spring alone, three summers later, with a little sack of coarse salt, the gift herders give to things they are afraid of. {He} puts it on the edge stone and sits down on the moss a long way off. "That winter," {he} says, "there was nothing in the house. I thought one ewe's price in grain from the widow, and nobody would know." Every word tastes of plain water.

choices.text: Leave the salt where it is, and lay your ears back to {him}

mem.note: bowed when I told the truth

effects.log: For the first time you bow to a liar, because just now {npc} is not one. {He} does not understand it, and then {he} does, and goes down the hill with {his} face working. {He} takes the salt home. You did not want it.

choices.text: Lick the salt

effects.log: It is very good salt. It is also a gift, and it was given to make you think well of the giver, and for a week afterward your bud is a little warm and slow. Gifts cloud. You knew that. (-2 Clarity)

choices.text: Listen to all of it, and say nothing

effects.log: The hungry winter, a sick child, the widow's dog barking at night. A liar is not only a liar. You lie there long after {npc} has gone, with that in your mouth, and it is not salt and not water, and you do not have a word for it yet.

events.text: {npc} is old now, and brings a grandchild up to the edge of the forest on a summer evening, and points into the birches. "In there," {he} says, "lives a beast with one horn that knows when you are lying. I know, because it knew when I was." The child peers into the trees with enormous eyes. So, from the trees, do you.

choices.text: Step out where the child can see you

effects.log: The child sees a grey-white beast with a short white horn standing in the birches, and you see a child who will tell this story to grandchildren of their own. The hamlet never lies at the edge of the forest again. It lies everywhere else, like everyone.

choices.text: Stay hidden. A story is better than a sight

effects.log: The child sees nothing but trees, and believes anyway, which is a kind of honesty too. {npc} laughs and takes the small hand and goes down to the hamlet in the dusk.

events.text: A stranger at your spring: a haechi so old its scales have gone the grey of lichen, one ear torn, its horn long and yellow as old ivory. It has come from beyond the river, it says, and is going north, to sit the Stone Sleep where its own mother sat it. It lies down on your moss without asking and drinks for a whole day. Nobody has ever made your spring look small before.
events.arc: The Judge With a Horse's Mouth

choices.text: Bring it bitter leaves from your tree

effects.log: It eats them slowly, one at a time, with its eyes closed. "A good tree," it says. "Somebody carried this one far." It does not say who. It does not need to.

choices.text: Ask it about the south

effects.log: "Rice," it says. "Walls. More people in one market than trees in your forest, and every one of them saying something." It looks at the bud on your brow. "You will be very busy."

choices.text: Lie down at a polite distance and wait

effects.log: You wait all day. At dusk it opens one eye and says, "Good. A haechi who can wait has half the trade already." The other half, it says, will take you a thousand years.

events.text: Night, fireflies over the water, and the old haechi tells you the oldest story. Long ago, in the Central Plains, a sage king had a minister who judged the people's quarrels: a man with a face the colour of a peeled melon and a mouth like a horse's, very wise, who could not tell guilt by looking. So he kept a one-horned beast, our ancestor, and when he could not tell, the beast lowered its head at the one in the wrong. "Every court in that country painted the two of them on its wall," the old one says. "The judge and the beast. Some walls still have us on them."
events.arc: The Judge With a Horse's Mouth

choices.text: Ask what the judge did with the guilty

effects.log: "Sentenced them," it says. "That was his. The pointing was ours. Remember that: we never once said what should be done. Only who." It is quiet for a while. "There are beasts who sentence. We are not those."

choices.text: Ask whether the ancestor was ever wrong

effects.log: "Once," the old one says. "And the judge believed the horn over his own eyes, because he had stopped using his eyes. That is the danger, kid. Not that we are wrong. That a court with a haechi in it stops thinking."

choices.text: Ask whether you will be painted on a wall

effects.log: The old one laughs, a sound like stones going down a well. "If you are good enough, on a great many walls," it says. "And every one of those pictures will be watching you. It is not as nice as it sounds."

events.text: The old haechi gets up in the grey before dawn and shakes its mane, and its long horn rings, low and cracked, like a bell that has been dropped once. "Two cracks," it says, seeing you hear it. "Both mended. It took two hundred years." Then it walks north, toward the ridge where the larches end.
events.arc: The Judge With a Horse's Mouth

choices.text: Walk with it as far as the ridge

effects.log: You walk all day at the pace of a very old beast. At the ridge it lies down beside a grey stone the shape of a lying haechi, and looks at the stone for a long time, and then at you. "Go south when you are grown," it says. "Somebody has to."

choices.text: Ask how it mended them

effects.log: "I went back," it says. "To the ones I wronged. Or their graves. Or their grandchildren, who did not know me from a stone lion. I lay at their gates until they forgave me. Some never did. Those were the ones that mended slowest, and best."

choices.text: Bow to it, ears back

effects.log: It stops, and looks at you, and bows back. Your ears are nearly flat now. They will be flat soon. It goes north into the dawn and you never see it again, and you think of it every time you shake your head.

events.text: The great river, frozen bank to bank, a white road a li wide with the wind running down it. South of it is the kingdom: villages, rice, law. To cross it is death, for a human: the law calls it crossing the border, and hangs the ones caught a third time. Men cross it anyway, at night, in the coldest weeks, with salt going north and ginseng coming south. You stand on the bank where their tracks go down onto the ice.

choices.text: Follow the smugglers' tracks: they know where the ice is thick

effects.log: Their tracks wind like a snake's across the white, round the dark patches where the current runs under, and you follow them exactly. By dawn you are on the south bank, and the smell of the world has changed: smoke, dung, millet, people.

choices.text: Cross alone, straight, by your own feet

ok.log: Straight across, by moonlight, with the ice singing under you. A frontier sentry on the south bluff sees a grey beast walk out of the north and up the bank, and does not report it, because who would believe him.

fail.log: Halfway, a dark patch you did not see, and you go through into black water that stops your heart. You get your forelegs on the edge and your horn bud into the ice and haul out, and lie on the white shaking. You cross the rest on your belly. (-15 health)

choices.text: Wait for the hardest cold, and cross at noon

effects.log: You wait eleven days on the north bank, chewing bark. On the twelfth the ice booms all night with cold, and at noon you walk across it like a road. The south bank smells of smoke and people.

events.text: A smugglers' fire in a gully on the south bank, ginseng bundles under a hide. They have stopped to divide the load, and the count is short one root, a good one, as long as a hand. The leader turns on the youngest. "Thief." {npc} goes white. "On my mother," {npc} says. "On my mother's grave, I did not touch it." Then they see you at the mouth of the gully, and nobody moves.

choices.text: "On my mother," {npc} says (the horn: true). The leader shouts that {npc} is a thief (the horn: a lie). Lower your head at the leader

effects.log: You walk through the firelight and lower your head at the leader, and the root slides out of the leader's own sleeve onto the snow. The others look at it, and at the leader, and at you. {npc} sits down very suddenly, as if {his} knees had gone.

choices.text: The horn is cold and silent. Lie down on the snow between them until they stop

effects.log: You lie down between the leader and {npc} and do not lower your head at anyone. It is very hard to beat a boy with a beast lying in the way. In the end they divide the load short, and grumble, and nobody is beaten. You do not know who took it. Better no butt than a wrong one.

choices.text: Lower your head at {npc}, who is shaking

effects.log: Shaking is not guilt. You know that now, too late. The leader beats {npc} and takes {his} share and leaves {him} on the bank, and walks away with the root still hidden in that same sleeve. Something in your horn cracks. (A crack: -8 Clarity)

choices.text: Go round the gully. Smugglers' quarrels are their own

effects.log: You go round. Behind you, voices, a blow, a long silence. In the spring you will find the place, and nothing there but the ashes of a fire.

events.text: Torches on the south bluff: a frontier patrol, out on a cold night because a beast was reported on the ice. Below them, in the reeds, the smugglers lie flat with their loads. If they are found on this bank with ginseng from the other, they hang. The patrol is coming down the path, and you are standing in the open between the reeds and the torches.

choices.text: Walk up the path toward the torches, slowly, and let them see you

ok.log: The patrol sees a grey beast with a white horn in their torchlight, and stops, and argues, and goes back up to the fort to report it to somebody braver. Behind you the reeds empty, very quietly, south.

fail.log: A frightened soldier looses an arrow, and it takes you across the shoulder. The patrol chases you along the bank half the night. The smugglers get away. You are not sure they deserved it, and you are bleeding. (-12 health)

choices.text: Stay out of it. A law is not a lie

effects.log: You go downriver in the dark. You do not see what the patrol finds. A haechi does not sentence, and does not save anyone from a sentence; you tell yourself that, and it is true, and it tastes of nothing at all.

choices.text: Walk into the reeds and lie down beside the smugglers

effects.log: The torches come down to the river and swing over the reeds, and light on a grey beast lying there with its eyes shining, and the patrol decides at once that there is nothing in these reeds but a beast. They are wrong. They are, for once, glad to be.

events.text: A frontier post on the bluff above the river: a wall of field stone, a gate, thirty soldiers, and on the hill above it the beacon mound, where one fire at night means all is well and more than one means the enemy has crossed. The soldiers have seen you about. Somebody leaves a heap of millet at the gate. Somebody else, the same week, sets a snare.

choices.text: Eat the millet, leave the snare

effects.log: Millet is sweet, after bark. It is also a gift. The snare you step over is a gift too, of another kind. Between them you learn that a fort is not one thing. (-1 Clarity)

choices.text: Lie on the slope above and watch the beacon every night

effects.log: One fire, every night, all winter. Except three nights in the middle of the cold, when the beacon is dark and nobody on the wall seems to notice.

choices.text: Keep away. Soldiers are soldiers

effects.log: You keep to the far side of the river bend. The bugle comes to you on the wind every dawn. You find you know the soldiers' voices anyway, by spring, as you know the birds.

events.text: They bring {npc} back to the post with {his} hands tied: a young soldier, caught on the south road two days' walk from the fort. To leave a frontier post is death. "I was sent," {npc} says to the commander, again and again, "with a message to the county." The commander says there was no message. The soldiers look at you, lying in the snow by the gate, because by now the whole post knows what you are.

choices.text: "I was sent with a message," says {npc} (the horn: a lie). Lower your head at {him}

effects.log: You get up and lower your head at {npc}, and {he} sags in the ropes, and the commander nods as if that settles it. The truth is the truth. Then you see the commander's face, and taste it, and it is salt all the way down.

choices.text: Know it is a lie, and lay your horn on the ground

effects.log: You know, and you lay your head down on your forepaws with the horn on the snow, and do not point. The soldiers murmur: the beast will not say. The commander has to decide alone, and puts it off till the inspector comes. It is the first time you keep a truth. It is heavy. (-3 Clarity)

choices.text: The horn is silent. Watch the commander instead

effects.log: The commander does not look at {npc}. The commander looks at the beacon mound on the hill, and back, and wipes a dry mouth. Your horn tells you nothing; your eyes tell you something is wrong on that hill.

choices.text: Get up and walk away. This is the fort's business

effects.log: You go. Behind you the gate closes. All that night you lie on the slope above, and the beacon on the mound is lit, one fire, all is well, and you do not believe it.

events.text: The truth comes out in pieces, at night, through the wall of the lock-up where {npc} is held, talking to the dark or to you. Three nights in the cold the commander slept in the warm room and nobody lit the beacon. Raiders came over the ice and burned a hamlet upriver. {npc} went south at a run to tell the county, because the commander would not. The truth would hang {npc} for leaving the post. The lie would hang the post.

choices.text: The commander swears the beacon was lit every night (the horn: a lie). Lower your head at the commander before the whole post

effects.log: At the morning muster you walk through the ranks and lower your head at the commander, and keep it lowered, and walk the commander backwards to the foot of the beacon mound. Nobody stops you. When the county inspector comes in spring, the whole post tells the inspector everything, all at once.

choices.text: Lie down at the lock-up door, beside {npc}, every night until the inspector comes

mem.note: lay at my door all winter

effects.log: Nobody can take {npc} out to be hanged with a beast lying across the door. The soldiers bring you millet and pretend not to. The inspector comes in spring and asks the right questions, because the whole post is waiting to be asked. (-6 health)

choices.text: Your horn is clean enough to read both at once: the message was a lie (the horn: a lie), the reason for it was true (the horn: true). Wait for the inspector, and lie down between {npc} and the commander

effects.log: When the county inspector comes, the soldiers watch where you lie: between the two of them, your horn toward the commander, your ears laid back toward {npc}. A lie and a truth inside one man, and a liar in the warm room. The inspector is not a fool. {npc} is sent home in disgrace and alive; the commander is not sent home at all.

choices.text: The horn cannot reach so deep. Leave it to the inspector

effects.log: You go back across the river. Later, from a salt peddler on the ice, you hear that the inspector came, and somebody was punished, and you do not know who. That will happen to you often. It never gets easier.

events.text: Years later, at the ford, a traveller with a limp and a soldier's way of looking at a riverbank: {npc}, older, with a pack and a walking stick and grey in {his} topknot. {He} stops when {he} sees you, and stands there a long time. "The new commander lights the beacon every night," {he} says at last. "Every night. I made sure."

choices.text: Lay your ears back and bow to {him}

mem.note: bowed to me at the ford

effects.log: {npc} bows back, soldier-stiff, then sits down on the bank and laughs until {he} has to wipe {his} eyes. "They will never believe me at the inn," {he} says. They do not. {He} tells them anyway, every winter.

choices.text: Walk beside {him} across the ford

effects.log: The ford is deep in the middle and {npc} limps. You walk on the upstream side and take the current on your flank, and {he} holds your mane, and neither of you says anything, and it is enough.

events.text: Up the valley there is a cave that smells of mugwort and wild garlic, and in it lives a bear so old it is white round the muzzle. The forest says it is a spirit. It has never told a lie in its life, the forest says, which is not as hard as it sounds, because it has hardly ever said anything at all. You climb up to see.

choices.text: Sit at the cave mouth and wait for it to speak

effects.log: You sit from morning to dusk. The bear looks at you once, at noon. At dusk it says, "Hm," and goes back into the dark. Your bud tastes nothing at all, and you have never been so rested.

choices.text: Ask it a question

effects.log: You ask why it never speaks. It considers the question for so long that a snowdrift builds up against your flank. Then it says, "Mostly I have nothing to say," and that is true, and somehow very funny.

choices.text: Bring it a bundle of bitter leaves

effects.log: It sniffs them, eats one, makes a face, and eats the rest. Something passes between you that is not words. Bitter-eaters know each other.

events.text: Two jays quarrel in the pine below the cave about a hoard of nuts: whose it was, who moved it, who is a liar. You can taste it from here: the younger jay is lying. You get up to go down. The old bear puts one paw on your back, very heavy, and says the longest sentence you will ever hear from it: "Not every truth is yours to say."

choices.text: Sit back down under the paw

effects.log: The jays quarrel themselves out by dusk and share the nuts, grumbling. Nobody needed a horn. You sit under the bear's paw and think about that until the stars come out.

choices.text: Go anyway. A lie is a lie

effects.log: You go down and lower your head at the younger jay, and it confesses, and the older jay takes all the nuts, and the two never speak again. When you climb back up the bear is asleep. You were right. You lie awake wondering what it cost.

choices.text: Ask it how you will know which truths are yours

effects.log: The bear thinks about it until the snow stops. "When it is heavy to keep," it says, "it may be yours to keep. When it is heavy to say, it may be yours to say." Then it goes to sleep for the winter, having said more than it meant to.

events.text: Spring, and the old bear does not come out of the cave. You go in. It is lying at the back on a bed of dry mugwort, breathing slowly, older than it was. "Waited a hundred days in here once," it says, "for something." It does not say what. "Came out a bear anyway. That was right too." Then it is quiet.

choices.text: Lie beside it in the dark until it sleeps

effects.log: You lie in the mugwort smell with the great slow breathing beside you, and say nothing, and it is the most honest season of your life. In autumn the cave is empty, and the forest says the bear has gone up into the mountain. You say nothing. (+2 Clarity)

choices.text: Ask what it waited for

effects.log: It opens one eye. "To be something else," it says. "Did not want it enough. Wanted to be a bear more." The eye closes. You carry that answer south with you, and do not understand it for a very long time.

events.text: A child from the charcoal-burners' huts down the valley comes to your spring for water, because it is the clearest in the hills: {npc}, with a jar on {his} back and bare feet. {He} kneels to fill the jar and stops, and stares into the water, and touches {his} own face. The reflection is crooked. Not much. As if seen through old glass. You have noticed it before, with the fox.

choices.text: Lie still on the far bank and let {him} look

effects.log: {npc} looks a long time. "I told my mother I fed the hens," {he} says to the water, very quietly. "I did not." The reflection goes straight. {He} looks up and sees you, and does not run, because a child who has just told the truth to a spring has nothing left to be afraid of.

choices.text: Come round to {his} side and look into the water with {him}

effects.log: Your reflection and {npc}'s, side by side. Yours is straight. {His} own is crooked. {He} looks from one to the other and goes red to the ears and says, to you, "The hens." You do not know what it means. You lay your ears back anyway.

choices.text: Stir the water with your hoof so the picture breaks

effects.log: The picture breaks into ripples, and {npc} sighs with relief, and fills the jar, and goes. But {he} will be back. Children always come back to a thing that knows something about them.

events.text: {npc} comes every morning now to check. Some mornings the reflection is straight, and {he} fills the jar humming. Some mornings it is crooked, and {he} sits on the moss and thinks, and goes home, and comes back at noon, and it is straight. Today {he} kneels, and it is very crooked, and {he} does not move.

choices.text: Wait. {He} will tell the water when {he} is ready

effects.log: It takes until noon. Then {npc} says to the water that {he} broke the burner's best bowl and said the cat did it, and the cat was beaten. {He} cries. The reflection goes straight. {He} goes home to tell them, which is much harder than telling a spring.

choices.text: Lower your head, very gently, at the water

effects.log: {npc} looks at you and understands: the beast knows too. {He} goes home without the water, straight to the burners' hut, and you hear, very faintly, a child confessing, and an adult laughing, and a cat being given a whole fish.

choices.text: Muddy the spring a little, so {he} cannot see

effects.log: Kind, perhaps. {npc} goes home relieved. But your own water is cloudy for three days, and so is your horn, and a spring that shows nothing is only a puddle. (-2 Clarity)

events.text: Years later {npc} comes up the valley grown, with a child of {his} own on {his} hip, and kneels at your spring, and looks. It is straight. It has been straight, {he} tells you, without any reason to think you understand, for years. "I check anyway," {he} says. "Every spring. In case."

choices.text: Lay your ears back and bow to {him}

effects.log: {npc} bows back, and then holds the child out over the water to see, and the child sees a straight little face and a grey beast with a white horn, and shrieks with joy. The burners' children will come to this spring to check their faces for a hundred years.

choices.text: Show the child the spring, too

effects.log: The child leans so far over the water that you have to hold the back of their jacket in your teeth. Their reflection is perfectly straight. Children under three, you have learned, have not yet thought of anything to lie about.

events.text: Two wolves of the valley pack over one kill on the frozen stream: a lean young male with a torn ear, and the old grey she-wolf with her one pup of the year behind her legs. "My pup brought it down," says the old one. The pup is the size of a hare. The young male says he ran it for half a day. The pack waits for the young haechi who has come down to the stream to drink.

choices.text: The old wolf says her pup made the kill (the horn: a lie). Lower your head at her, gently

effects.log: You lower your head at the old wolf and push her, not hard, into the snow. She gets up and looks at you with no anger at all, only tiredness. The kill goes to the young male. He eats, and then, without being asked, he leaves the pup a leg.

choices.text: Lower your head at the old wolf on the look of the pup alone

ok.log: A pup that size could not bring down a hare, never mind a deer. You do not need a horn for that; you need eyes. The old wolf goes over in the snow and does not argue. The young male eats first and leaves the pup a leg.

fail.log: You hesitate, and the old wolf sees you hesitate, and snaps at your nose for your trouble. The pack drifts off. Nobody eats in peace. (-5 health)

choices.text: She is lying for her pup. Let the lie stand

effects.log: You turn and drink and do not look at anyone. The old wolf feeds her pup. The young male goes away hungry over the ridge, and it is a hard winter, and you will think about him in it. (-1 Clarity)

events.text: A hard month. The young wolf with the torn ear has been driven out of the pack and is hunting alone along the ridge, too thin, and the old she-wolf is lame and cannot hunt at all, and her pup is crying in the den. They both come to your spring to drink on the same evening, and stop on opposite sides, and look at each other.

choices.text: Lie down between them, ears back, as if to two upright beasts

effects.log: Neither of them is quite upright. Both are trying. You lay your ears back to both, and something in the young male's shoulders comes down, and that week he brings a hare to the den. A lie told and a truth shown, and a pack mended between them.

choices.text: Leave them to it. Wolves have their own law

effects.log: They drink, and part, and that is all. In spring there are three wolves together on the ridge, one lame, one torn-eared, one half-grown. You do not know how it happened. Not everything needs a horn.

events.text: The pup is grown and leads the valley pack, a big grey wolf with its mother's tired eyes. It comes to your spring one evening alone. "She lied for me," it says. "I know it now. I used to think I brought that deer down." It looks at your horn. "Was she wrong?"

choices.text: Tell it the truth: she lied, and she was not wrong to love you

effects.log: "Both?" says the wolf. "Both," you say. It thinks about that the way wolves think, with its whole body, and then lies down at the far side of your spring for the night, as if it has been told something it can live with.

choices.text: Tell it only that the young wolf ran that deer for half a day

effects.log: The wolf is quiet a long time. Then it gets up and goes up the ridge, to where the old torn-eared wolf lies in the sun these days, too slow to hunt, and lies down beside him. It is the pack's business how that ends. It ends well.

events.text: Five diggers come up into the deep hills in white clothes, with long staffs and a pot and nothing else. They have kept apart from their villages for a week to come up clean, without meat, so the mountain spirit will show them a root. At a little altar of piled stones under an old pine they set out a bowl of rice and a cup of clear water and kneel, and swear by the old rule: whoever sees a root first marks every root in sight, and calls; the rest dig only what is unmarked; and nobody hides anything from anyone. The mountain is listening. So are you.

choices.text: Lie down above the altar and listen to the oath

effects.log: Five voices, five oaths. Four of them taste of cold water. The fifth, {npc}, the one with the newest staff, swears just as loud, and it tastes of nothing yet, because {he} has not broken it yet. You will watch {him}.

choices.text: Drink the cup of clear water they left for the mountain

effects.log: When they come back from their first day the cup is empty, and there are cloven hoof prints by the altar with one scrape between them. The eldest goes very quiet and prays twice as long. {npc} laughs, and nobody laughs with {him}. (+2 Clarity)

choices.text: Go further up and leave them to their mountain

effects.log: You go up into the fog. All week you hear them below, the staffs tapping the ferns, and on the fourth day a voice crying out the old cry over the hills: found it! Found it! It is a rule as much as a shout.

events.text: The eldest found a root and called the cry and marked it with red thread, and the others dug what was unmarked. But in a hollow under a rotten log, out of sight of the rest, {npc} found an old root, five-pronged, worth a farm, and it went into {his} sleeve. Tonight at the altar, by the old rule, each digger swears again that they hid nothing. {npc} kneels last.

choices.text: {npc} swears {he} found nothing (the horn: a lie). Walk down to the altar and lower your head at {him}

effects.log: Five diggers see a horned beast walk out of the fog onto the altar stones and lower its head at the one with the newest staff. The root falls out of {npc}'s sleeve into the rice bowl. Nobody touches it for a long time. In the morning, by the rule, it is shared six ways, and the sixth share is left on the altar.

choices.text: The horn is fogged. Lie down by the altar so they all must swear in front of you

effects.log: They swear in front of a haechi, one by one. {npc} kneels last, and stops, and the words do not come out. Nobody needed a horn. In the morning {npc} lays the five-pronged root on the altar stones and walks down the mountain alone.

choices.text: Let the mountain settle its own oath

effects.log: You stay in the trees. That night the fog comes down so thick the diggers cannot see the altar, and {npc} gets up in the night and does not find the hut again till dawn, soaked, shaking, and short one five-pronged root, which is somewhere in the fog where {he} dropped it.

events.text: The fog does not lift. Three days now, so thick the diggers cannot find the path down, and the rice is gone. The eldest says the mountain spirit is angry: somebody broke the oath. They sit in the hut and look at each other. You know the way down. You know every way down.

choices.text: Walk past the hut, slowly, close enough to be followed

ok.log: They follow the grey shape in the fog for a day, holding each other's belts, and come out above their own village at dusk. The eldest bows to the fog. Next year there is a second bowl on the altar, a small one, with bitter leaves in it.

fail.log: You lose them in the fog twice and have to go back. It takes two days. Everyone gets down, cold and starving and furious with each other. (-8 health)

choices.text: Wait until {npc} goes up to the altar alone and confesses

effects.log: On the fourth morning {npc} climbs to the altar alone and kneels and says it out loud, to the stones, all of it. The fog lifts by noon. You did not do anything. You did not need to. The mountain has its own horn.

events.text: Years later, a digger's party at the old altar, and leading it is {npc}, grey now, with a staff worn smooth. {He} sets out the rice and the clear water, and a second, small bowl of bitter leaves beside them, and tells the young ones the rule. Then {he} tells them about the night {he} broke it, which is not part of the rule, and which {he} tells every year.

choices.text: Show yourself on the slope above the altar

effects.log: The young ones see a grey-white beast with one horn standing in the old pines, and their mouths fall open. {npc} only nods to you, as to an old acquaintance. That season nobody on that mountain hides a root.

choices.text: Eat the bitter leaves, and leave the rice

effects.log: In the morning the small bowl is empty and the big one is not, and {npc} smiles all day. It becomes the rule on that mountain: rice for the spirit, bitter leaves for the beast who listens. (+2 Clarity)

events.text: At the ford a thin monk in a patched grey robe is sitting on a stone, eating cold millet out of his alms bowl with his fingers. He sees you and does not run. "I am not holy," he says, as if you had asked. "I am a monk who is bad at it. I eat too fast and I fall asleep in the chanting and I have never once seen the Buddha." Every word tastes of clear, cold water. Your ears, which have never once done it, go flat back against your skull.

choices.text: Bow to him, as you once saw it done for the upright

effects.log: You lower your head with your ears laid flat, and the monk stops eating, and puts the bowl down, and bows back, a long, careful bow, as if to someone important. "Well," he says. "Nobody has ever done that before." Neither has anybody done it to you.

choices.text: Sniff the alms bowl

effects.log: He offers it to you. It is cold millet with a pickled radish on top. You eat the radish. He laughs, a terrible laugh like a goose, and your ears stay flat the whole time, because even his laugh is true.

choices.text: Ask him with your eyes what holy is, then

effects.log: "Something that is the same all the way through, I think," he says, looking into the bowl. "Like this millet. It is not good, but it is millet all the way down." He finishes it. Your ears do not come up till he has gone.

events.text: The monk builds a hermitage of brushwood above the ford and stays. The villagers below start calling him holy, and bringing rice. He tells them he is not, and they take it for humility and bring more. Then a rich man from the market town comes up with a cart of offerings and says, before the whole village, that he gives only out of pure devotion and asks for nothing in return. He means a monopoly on the ford ferry.

choices.text: The rich man says he asks for nothing (the horn: a lie). Lie down across the cart's path

effects.log: The cart cannot pass a lying haechi. The rich man pushes, shouts, and finally, red in the face, says what he wants: the ferry. The monk says the ford does not belong to him to give. The villagers, who heard all of it, stop calling the monk holy and start calling him honest, which suits him better.

choices.text: Bow to the monk, before them all, and not to the rich man

effects.log: Everyone sees the beast with the horn lay its ears back to the monk, and walk past the rich man as if he were a post. They work out the rest themselves. People are better at that than horns give them credit for.

choices.text: Stay out of it. It is the monk's affair

effects.log: The monk sends the cart back himself, every grain of it. "I would only eat it too fast," he says. The rich man goes away offended, and the ferry stays free, and nobody needed you at all.

events.text: The monk is old now and dying in the brushwood hermitage, and the villagers are already arguing about the stupa they will build for his relics. He calls you in with a crooked finger. "Tell them," he whispers, "that I was not holy." You cannot speak to humans. Not yet. He knows it, and smiles.

choices.text: Lie at the hermitage door through the funeral with your ears up, not back

effects.log: All through the rites your ears stay up, as for any honest man, not flat as for a saint. The villagers notice. The stupa they build is very small, of river stones, and on it someone carves: he ate too fast. It is the truest stupa in the province.

choices.text: Lay your ears flat back anyway. He was the same all the way through

effects.log: You bow, ears flat, at his door, and the villagers see it and build a great stupa and call him holy for three hundred years. You were right, and he was right, and you are not sure which of you won.

events.text: A valley of charcoal kilns: humps of field stone and earth among the oaks, each with a little chimney, each breathing smoke for a week while the oak inside turns to charcoal. The burners live in huts beside them and read the coming charcoal from the colour of the smoke. It is warm in this valley in winter, the only warm place for fifty li. The smoke gets into everything.

choices.text: Stay the winter for the warmth

effects.log: Warm all winter, for the first time in your life. By spring your mane smells like a kitchen and your bud is grey with smoke, and when a burner swears his kiln is the best in the valley you cannot tell if it is true. It probably is not. (-5 Clarity)

choices.text: Pass through quickly with your head low

effects.log: A day of smoke in your eyes, and then clean snow on the far side. Your bud aches for a week. You will remember that smoke does something to a horn that cold never does. (-1 Clarity)

choices.text: Go round by the ridge, a long way

effects.log: Three extra days over bare rock in the wind. From the ridge you look down at the valley lying in its blue haze like a lake, and are glad not to be in it.

events.text: A quarrel at the biggest kiln: the kiln master says a boy stole a sack of charcoal in the night and sold it in the market town; the boy says he never left the hut. The burners have seen you about, and send for you. You stand in the smoke between them, and your horn is grey and thick and tells you nothing at all.

choices.text: Admit it to yourself: the horn cannot see. Lie down and point at nobody

effects.log: The burners wait. You lie down with your head on your forepaws. In the end the kiln master shrugs and docks the boy a day's rice, and the boy goes off swearing. You do not know who was right. You do know you were not wrong. (+1 Clarity)

choices.text: Guess. The boy's eyes are shifty

ok.log: You lower your head at the boy, and he bursts into tears and confesses: a sack, for his sick sister's medicine. It was a guess, and a lucky one. You do not feel lucky. You feel as if you crossed the river on thin ice.

fail.log: You lower your head at the boy, and he is beaten for it, and two days later the kiln master's own nephew is caught with the money. A crack, through the smoke. (-8 Clarity)

choices.text: Go out of the smoke and come back with a clean horn

effects.log: You walk up out of the valley into the wind and wash your head in a snow-melt stream until the grey runs out, and come back at dusk. By then the boy has run away, and the kiln master has found the sack under his own cart. Nobody needed you. Next time, come clean. (+3 Clarity)

events.text: Out of the kiln valley at last, sitting by a snow-melt pool with smoke still in your mane. Your bud feels like a dirty window. You think of the forest fire, and of a grey horn in a grey valley that could not tell a boy from a thief. Fire is not only fire. Its smoke is a kind of lie.

choices.text: Wash in the pool and chew bitter leaves until you are clean

effects.log: A month of it. The smoke comes out of your mane last. When the horn is clean again you shake your head, and it rings, and you promise yourself you will never be warm that way again. You will break the promise, in a city, for a better reason. (+5 Clarity)

choices.text: Sit the Stone Sleep by the pool for a season

effects.log: You sit so still that a wagtail nests on your back. When you stir, the moss cracks off your scales, and the smoke has gone out of your horn along with half a summer. (+3 Clarity)

events.text: Over the ridge, at the next spring north, there is another young haechi: a kid with a horn bud just like yours, only a little longer, which they mention at once. You meet on the ridge between the two springs. Nobody says anything sensible. By noon you are butting each other, horn bud to horn bud, over nothing at all, and you keep it up for a week.
events.arc: The Kid at the Far Spring

choices.text: Butt until one of you falls over

ok.log: They fall over first, on the fourth day, and get up laughing, and knock you over on the fifth. By the end of the week neither of you can remember what the quarrel was about, and both of you have sore brows and the best week of your lives.

fail.log: You fall over first, on the third day, and the fourth, and the fifth. They are very gracious about it. Unbearably gracious. (-4 health)

choices.text: Stop and taste whether they are telling the truth about the horn

effects.log: "Mine is longer." Salt. Just a little. You say so. They go red to the curls, then laugh, and admit it is the same length, and you measure them against a birch, and it is. Neither of you has ever had a friend who could catch you lying. It is wonderful.

choices.text: Refuse to butt, and lie down on the ridge

effects.log: They butt you twice, puzzled, and then lie down too, and the two of you lie on the ridge all afternoon looking at the two springs, yours and theirs, and arguing about which is clearer. Yours is. They say theirs is. Salt.

events.text: The haechi of the far spring has a game: they tell you three things, and one is a lie, and you must find it. Then you tell them three. Your horns are young, and the lies are small: a jay that does not exist, a frozen waterfall that is not frozen. You play it all summer on the ridge between the springs.
events.arc: The Kid at the Far Spring

choices.text: Play to win

effects.log: By autumn you can find their lie before they finish the second sentence, and they can find yours before you start. The game becomes impossible, and so you play it harder. (+2 Clarity)

choices.text: Tell them three true things, and let them hunt for a lie that is not there

effects.log: They look at you for a long time, and taste each sentence twice, and finally say, outraged, "There is no lie." "No," you say. They knock you into the spring. It is the best trick anyone has ever played on a haechi.

choices.text: Ask them what they will do when they are grown

effects.log: "Stay here," they say. "Keep the spring. Settle the frontier quarrels so quietly nobody ever knows." No salt at all. You realise you had expected them to say "go south", like you, and are surprised how much it matters.

events.text: One spring you go up to the ridge between the springs, to say what you have not said. The haechi of the far spring is already there, lying on the warm stone, as if they knew. Perhaps they did; a haechi is hard to surprise. "The south is full of liars," they say. "You will be very happy."
events.arc: The Kid at the Far Spring

choices.text: Ask them to come south with you

effects.log: "Not yet," they say, and it is true. "Somebody has to keep the frontier springs. If you lie down somewhere for long enough, I will come and find you." That is true too. You go south with it in your mouth like a cold stone.

choices.text: Butt them once more, for luck

effects.log: Horn to horn, both of them longer now. Neither falls over. You stand there pushing until you are both laughing, and then you go south, and every time your brow aches in the cold you think of the ridge.

choices.text: Go without saying goodbye. It is easier

effects.log: You go before dawn. From the river, looking back, you see a small grey shape on the ridge, watching you go. Nothing about it is a lie. You keep walking.

events.text: Your brow itches for a month, so badly that you rub it on every birch in the valley until the bark is polished. Then one morning the bud splits the curls and stands up, a finger long and white. You shake your head, and it rings, clearer than it has ever rung: a small clear note, like ice tapped with a stone, that goes out across the spring and comes back off the ridge.
