choices.text: Shake your head again and again to hear it

effects.log: Ring, and ring, and the jays come to see what kind of bird it is. By evening you have a headache and an echo in your skull, and the forest, when it talks, sounds a little more like what it means. (+2 Clarity)

choices.text: Hold very still and listen to what it rings at

effects.log: It rings faintly when the fox passes. It rings faintly when you remember telling the haechi of the far spring that your horn was longer. It does not ring at all at the spring. A horn, you discover, is an ear for something that is not sound. (+1 Clarity)

choices.text: Go and show someone

effects.log: There is nobody much to show. You show the magpie, who is unimpressed, and the snake, who is not there, and in the end a hare, who sits up and looks at your horn for a long moment and then, very slowly, lays its ears back.

events.text: The horn is a hand long now and as white as a candle, like the one you were born under. It rings at lies without your asking, and once, terribly, it rang at the old bear's cave when nobody was speaking, and you understood that it was ringing at you: something you had been telling yourself. You are not a kid any more.

choices.text: Find out what you have been telling yourself

effects.log: That you were going south for the quarrels. That you were not afraid of fire. That the squirrel, or the boy, or whoever it was, deserved it. You lie by the spring a long time saying the true versions to the water, and the horn goes quiet. (+3 Clarity)

choices.text: Shake your head until it stops

effects.log: It stops. It always stops, if you shake hard enough. You notice that, and do not like noticing it. (-2 Clarity)

choices.text: Lie in the spring with only the horn above the water

effects.log: You lie there till the stars come out, horn up like a white reed, and let the cold water wash out everything you have told yourself this year. It rings once, very softly, and then not at all. (+2 Clarity)

events.text: South of the river the forest thins and then stops, and there are fields: water standing in squares, green shoots in rows so straight they look like a lie, though they are not, and people bent over them up to the knee in mud, singing. Everything smells of dung and cooking and wet earth. A child on a dyke sees you and drops a whole basket of frogs.

choices.text: Walk along the dykes in the open

effects.log: The singing stops field by field as you pass, and starts again behind you, louder, and different: a song about a beast with one horn. By evening the whole valley has decided what you are, and is half right.

choices.text: Keep to the hills and watch the fields from above

effects.log: From the hill you can hear everything. Rice farmers argue all day about water: who opened whose sluice in the night. Half of it is salt. You have never in your life been so busy without moving.

choices.text: Help the child pick up the frogs

effects.log: You nose the frogs back toward the basket, one at a time, and the child stops screaming and starts laughing, and goes home and tells everyone, and nobody believes a word of it.

events.text: Night, and two farmers are standing in a dark paddy shouting about water. The upper field's sluice was opened in the night and the lower field is dry and cracking. The upper farmer says the sluice gate rotted and fell open by itself. The lower farmer says nobody's sluice rots in a night. They see your horn in the moonlight, and both of them point at the other.

choices.text: The upper farmer says the gate rotted open by itself (the horn: a lie). Lower your head at him

effects.log: You lower your head at the upper farmer, and he sits down in his own paddy, and says he opened it for his seedlings, just for one night, just this once. The lower field gets its water by morning. Two families stop speaking for a generation. That is not your business. The water was.

choices.text: Your horn is muddled by all the people. Go and look at the sluice gate

ok.log: The gate is sound oak, wet, with a fresh mark where a mattock lifted it. You stand beside it until the farmers come and look. Then it is very quiet in the paddy.

fail.log: It is dark, and a sluice is a sluice, and you cannot tell anything. The farmers argue till dawn and take it to the village headman, who is the upper farmer's cousin. You learn something about villages.

choices.text: Lie down across the ditch so the water runs back to the lower field

effects.log: You lie in the ditch like a dam, which is undignified and cold and works. The water goes where it was meant to go. Both farmers stand and look at you, and then, oddly, at each other, and go home without another word.

events.text: A market town on the river, on market day: salt, sickles, dried fish, straw shoes, a man selling medicine for every illness from one jar. Everyone is telling a small lie. The fish are fresh; the sickles are the best iron; the medicine is a secret of the mountain hermits. Your horn rings so much you can hardly hear.

choices.text: Walk through the market slowly, horn up

effects.log: Where you walk, the prices go down and the fish get older. By noon the medicine seller has packed up and left town. By evening the market has decided that a haechi is very bad for business, and very good for buying.

choices.text: Leave quickly. Your horn cannot bear it

effects.log: Out of the gate and up into the hills, with the horn ringing like a struck bowl. It takes three days by a cold stream to stop. You will have to learn to live in that noise, if you are going where you think you are going. (+1 Clarity)

choices.text: Your horn is clean enough to sort them: listen only for the lies that harm (the horn: clear)

effects.log: Under the hundred little lies, three that matter: a short weight on the salt scale, a sickle of soft iron sold as hard, and the medicine that is only river clay. You stand by each stall in turn until the town works it out. The fresh fish that are not fresh you let alone. Somebody has to eat them.

choices.text: Lie at the gate all day and listen, to learn the kinds of lie

effects.log: Lies to sell, lies to be liked, lies to be left alone, lies out of habit, lies out of kindness. Most of them, you notice, harm nobody. A few of them harm everybody. The trade, you begin to suspect, is in telling which. (-1 Clarity)

events.text: From a high pass, on a very clear autumn morning, you see further south than you have ever seen: ridge after ridge going blue, a great river shining, and on the very edge of the world, small and sharp, a mountain whose peaks stand up like the tongues of a flame. You look at it for a long time. Your horn is quite silent. But your mouth tastes of smoke.

choices.text: Stare at it until the sun is high

effects.log: It does not move. Mountains do not. But you have the feeling, very strongly, that it has seen you too, and that one day you will lie down somewhere and look at it for a very long time.

choices.text: Turn your back on it and go down to the rice

effects.log: You go down. But the taste of smoke stays in your mouth all the way to the next valley, and that night you dream of a city burning, and of a bell.

choices.text: Lay your ears back to it, as to something you will have to understand

effects.log: It is not upright, and it is not a liar. It is fire, waiting. You lay your ears back anyway, out of respect, the way the wolves drink fast near a haechi.

events.text: In a village on the river a shaman reads truth in water: a bowl of the clean water drawn first at dawn, set on a low table, and she sees in it who stole, who lied, who brought the sickness. Today the headman's hen is missing, and the shaman bends over the bowl, and the water trembles, and she points at a widow's son. You are lying at the gate. You saw her knee knock the table.

choices.text: The shaman says the water shows the boy (the horn: a lie). Walk in and lower your head at her

effects.log: The courtyard empties backwards as you walk in. You lower your head at the shaman, and she drops the bowl, and the clean water runs across the yard, and in the silence somebody remembers seeing the hen in the headman's own cousin's yard. The boy goes home with his mother. The shaman leaves the village within the month.

choices.text: Walk in and knock the table yourself, so they all see the water shake

effects.log: You put your hoof on the table edge and the water trembles, exactly as before, and points nowhere. The villagers look at the table, and at the shaman's knee, and at each other. You did not need the horn. You needed a hoof and an audience.

choices.text: Lie still. The village must learn its own shamans

effects.log: They beat the boy and fine his mother a hen. In the night you go and stand at the shaman's gate, and she comes out and sees you, and goes white, and the next morning she finds the hen. She does not say where. (-1 Clarity)

events.text: In the next village there is another shaman, an old woman with a face like a walnut, who does not use a bowl at all. She sees you on the hill and walks up, slowly, on a stick, and sits down on a stone in front of you as if you were a neighbour. "So," she says. "You are the one who is going to lie down in front of a gate and look at a fire for a very long time." Your horn is utterly still. She is telling the truth, or she believes it.

choices.text: Lay your ears back and listen

effects.log: "Keep your horn clean," she says. "They will want it dirty. Every one of them, kings and all. And when it is dirty, they will say it is clean, because it suits them." She pats your nose like a calf's and goes down the hill. She has told you nothing you can use, and everything.

choices.text: Ask her with your eyes how she knows

effects.log: "I do not know," she says. "I see. It is not the same. You will learn the difference, and then you will be much less sure of yourself, and much better." She laughs, and every bit of the laugh is true.

choices.text: Lower your head at her: nobody can know such things

effects.log: She does not move. "You will have to do better than that," she says, gently, "to frighten a woman who has seen her own death." Your horn says nothing at all. You were not butting a liar. You were butting a thing you did not want to hear. (-3 Clarity)

events.text: The widow's son from the hen case, half grown now, finds you at the river with a bowl of his own: the clean water drawn first at dawn, carried all the way from the village without spilling. He sets it in front of you on a flat stone, the way his mother sets one out for the household spirits, and backs away, and kneels.

choices.text: Drink it

effects.log: It is the cleanest water you have tasted since the spring at the edge of the world. He watches you drink every drop with enormous satisfaction, and takes the bowl home, and his mother keeps it on the shelf for the rest of her life and never uses it for anything else. (+2 Clarity)

choices.text: Lay your ears back to him, and leave the water

effects.log: He takes the full bowl home with great care and pours it out under the village guardian post, so the posts will know. It becomes a custom in that village: one bowl of dawn water a year, for the beast that does not take bribes.

events.text: Somebody always brings a quarrel to the spring now. Today a badger and a boar, over a sett the boar says it dug itself, last autumn, with its own snout. The badger says it is a badger's sett, obviously, look at it. The jays have come to watch. The forest has learned that the beast at the clear spring settles things.

choices.text: The boar says it dug the sett itself (the horn: a lie). Lower your head at the boar

effects.log: You lower your head at the boar, and it grumbles off into the bracken to dig a wallow, which is what boars are actually good at. The badger goes home. The jays tell everyone.

choices.text: The horn is quiet today. Look at the sett, and at the boar's snout

ok.log: Badger claws all down the tunnel walls. Not a trace of earth on the boar's snout. You lower your head at the boar, and it goes. Eyes, it turns out, are a horn too, a slower one.

fail.log: It is a hole. You know nothing about holes. You lie down and refuse to judge, and the badger and the boar share the sett, furiously, for a whole summer. You hear about it every day.

choices.text: Send them both away: come back when one of them is ready to say it plainly

effects.log: They go, muttering. The next morning the boar comes back alone, very early, and says that it did not dig the sett, and is going to dig its own, and could you not tell the jays. You do not tell the jays. The jays find out anyway.

events.text: Two deer at the spring, a doe and a young stag, over a fawn: the doe says the stag knocked it into the stream; the stag says it was nowhere near. The fawn, soaked and indignant, says nothing. Everyone looks at the horn on your brow, and then, with growing impatience, at the rest of you.

choices.text: The stag says it was nowhere near (the horn: true). Lay your ears back to the stag

effects.log: You bow to the stag, and the doe goes very still, and then the fawn, under its breath, admits it fell in chasing a frog. The doe is so embarrassed she drinks for a long time. No butt at all, and every one of them knows the truth now.

choices.text: Ask the fawn

effects.log: The fawn looks at its mother, and at the stag, and at you, and bursts out that it was chasing a frog. Children, you are learning, will tell you everything if you ask them and nobody else is shouting.

choices.text: Lower your head at the stag. Young stags are rough

effects.log: The stag goes into the stream from your butt, and comes out, and walks away without a word, and the fawn starts crying, and confesses about the frog. A crack, for a stag who was nowhere near. (-8 Clarity)

events.text: A wet spring, a crowded spring: every creature in the valley has a grievance this year, and they bring them all to you. A jay accuses another jay. A hare accuses a hare. A raven, for reasons of its own, accuses the weather. By noon you have heard nine cases and your horn feels like a well that has been drawn too often.

choices.text: Hear every case, till dark

effects.log: Nine cases, and you get seven right, and send two away for want of knowing. One of the seven was a real liar and the horn rang clean at it. By dark you are hoarse in a part of you that has no voice. (-2 Clarity)

choices.text: Hear none of them. Graze the bitter tree and come back tomorrow clean

effects.log: They wait, grumbling, and half of them settle it among themselves while you are gone. The other half are still there in the morning, and you are clean, and the horn rings true at the first lie of the day. (+3 Clarity)

choices.text: Only hear the ones who are frightened

effects.log: Two hares and a young jay. The rest you send away. The frightened ones are always the ones nobody else will listen to, and the horn, it turns out, is kindest when it is choosy.
